text.en: Reuven's link to din is shown in his stone: the red odem stands for pure din, and its names in other languages, ruby and rubin, echo the name Reuven.
Since each month follows a shevet in the order of the degalim and a nasi's soul carries his whole shevet and month, Elitzur's and Shlumiel's sins pulled Tammuz and Av down into churban.

Machlokes was created on Monday, the day of division between the waters, and Korach's tikkun is hidden in the fact that the Monday song, by the sons of Korach, praises Yerushalayim, the place of unity.
The lower a place or time has fallen, the holier the sparks of Moshiach captive in it, so the months of mourning are exactly where the work of bringing Moshiach is greatest.
The months of geulah belong to the faithful meraglim: Kalev of Yehuda, source of Moshiach ben Dovid, with Nissan, and Yehoshua of Ephraim, source of Moshiach ben Yosef, with Tishrei.
A shlichus has two vessels, place and time; a trip to the country is a shlichus in place, and Tammuz and Av themselves are a shlichus in time.
Tzafra, morning, is named for the birds that sing then, and ramsha, evening, for the insects that sing at night, but a Jew is not limited and sings both by day and by night.

The Satmar Rav: every journey in the desert had its function, and because they waited seven days for Miriam the forty days of the meraglim ended exactly on Tisha B'Av, an ill-fated day; otherwise the whole episode might not have happened.

Since the churban began with Miriam's lashon hara, the great movement in recent decades to learn the laws of lashon hara is Hashem sending agents to repair this flaw as the time of the Geulah approaches.
A sefer the Mashgiach brings sees the same pattern at Sinai: Moshe added a day for more preparation and purity, so the forty days ended on Shiva Asar B'Tammuz and the luchos were broken.
The Mashgiach compares Tisha B'Av to a gifted bochur who could have become a great talmid chacham but went sour: he too is a 'mo'ed', can be brought back, and will become one of the greatest.
Days are like people: there are tzaddik days and rasha days, each person is rooted in his day, and when a rasha does teshuvah not only his soul but his day is transformed.
Building on Tosafos' 'hidden' gematria, the Mashgiach computes the hidden letters of the words Tisha B'Av and finds in them the third Beis HaMikdash.

The meraglim had a hidden root of good, and because their sin fell on Tisha B'Av, which also has a hidden root, the two combined to give them hope of a tikkun; this is why waiting for Miriam was a reward.
Hoping for Moshiach is a test of belief: since Moshiach brings even material good that everyone wants, one who is not eager for him shows that he does not really believe he is coming.

Korach's and Dasan and Aviram's quarrel was a premature attempt to bring the order of the world of tikkun, in which the Leviim and the firstborn would serve as Kohanim, as they were originally meant to.

The two orders of the shevatim reflect two worlds: Yehudah first in the present flawed world, Reuven first in the world of tikkun; so Tammuz, Reuven's month, is now fourth and bitter but will become the highest.
Because Dasan and Aviram represent the month of Tammuz, the Rema MiPano's view that they have a tikkun is also the promise that Tammuz will be transformed from grief to joy.
Balak, who sought to curse Klal Yisrael, carried within himself the seed of Moshiach through Ruth, so the parsha read in Tammuz holds blessings born out of curses.
Yiftach's demand to be leader was not ambition: as a 'Tammuz soul' he knew that Tammuz and the rejected souls like him belong on top, and that they hold the keys to the Geulah.

The Mashgiach reads the rule that the first day of Pesach falls on the weekday of Tisha B'Av as proof that a Jewish churban is never without geulah: it is planted by the geulah and exists to produce it.

He applies the halachic idea of ben yomo to the calendar: Nissan, every day of which is Rosh Chodesh according to the Shelah, is a 'yerach ben yomo', a month whose freshness never goes stale, mirroring Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael.
The shofar, the symbol of ingathering, equals with its milui the two notes karnei parah and yerach ben yomo together, showing that it unites the month of division with the month of geulah.

He explains that the Torah required kashering the vessels of Midian even when not ben yomo measure for measure: Bilam tried to make Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael lose its freshness, so Midian's forbidden taste never loses its own.

Reading nasheh as forgetting, the Mashgiach makes the gid hanasheh the forgotten neshamos that Yaakov lost to Esav, and Tisha B'Av, the gid hanasheh among the days of the year, the day of those souls.

Dina was destined from birth to bear Osnas, the wife of Yosef and mother of Moshiach ben Yosef, so that Shechem, which looks like Yaakov's loss, held a hidden spark of Moshiach; Shechem ben Chamor equals 'haMelech haMashiach ben Yosef' in gematria.
When Tisha B'Av falls on Shabbos and is pushed off, eating on that day is like eating the gid hanasheh in holiness, a sign of the time when Yaakov will no longer limp and the lost neshamos return.
From Parshas Shlach on, read as Tammuz is blessed, the Torah introduces a new kind of figure, tzaddikim who fell: the meraglim, Korach, Moshe at Mei Merivah, Zimri.
Following Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of place, time and soul, the Mashgiach argues that just as there are fallen souls, the Nephilim, there are fallen times, and the Three Weeks are such days.

Moshe told the meraglim to 'dig' because, per the Rama MiPano, the letters before those of 'anavim' spell the name of the Satan: these are the Satan's days, but good is hidden in them for one who digs.
The Three Weeks begin and end with Moshiach: on Shiva Asar B'Tammuz Rus conceived Oved, ancestor of Dovid, and Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av.
'Somech Hashem lechol hanoflim' equals Tammuz in gematria, since Tammuz has fallen to the ground, while Av is only bent over and matches 'zokef lechol hakefufim'.
Parshas Pinchas lists the korbanos of all the Yamim Tovim, read in the Three Weeks, because these days are destined to become holidays.
Lavan's soul was quickly rectified into Barzilai because of his righteous children and son-in-law, whose initials, Bilhah, Rachel, Zilpah, Leah and Yaakov, spell Barzilai.
Asaf calls the psalm of the Churban a song because the destruction of the building was itself a Father's mercy: had the anger not fallen on wood and stone, the whole nation would have been wiped out.
Avimi, whose name spells 'days of Av', was the one to grasp this, and his father's name Avuha, with hey before vav, hints that the vav-to-hey order of the curses is temporary.
Esav's kibud av is greater than Yaakov's precisely because it is external: Yaakov speaks to his father in the second person and needs no special clothes, because real closeness needs no veneer.

The Gemara learns from goyim of Ashkelon because the Pelishtim there did not know their true fathers; lacking the natural bond, they honored their fathers as kings, which a loving Jewish home would not do.

The question 'how far does kibud av reach' asks about the mitzvah's greatness, and the answer is that the Satan himself pushes the goyim to excel in it, which shows how much depends on it, including the rebuilding of the Beis HaMikdash.

Kibud av and the longing for Eretz Yisrael are one thing, since both are bonds to one's origin, and this is why Yaakov feared Esav for exactly these two mitzvos and why the reward of kibud av is long life in the land.

Tamuz's letter combination is the only one fully reversed and taken from final letters, and the fact that it comes from the Megillah of 'v'nahapoch hu' shows that the month's purpose is to be transformed.

The Mashgiach adds that 'v'chol zeh einenu shoveh li', the source of the Tamuz combination, equals 'yemei bikurei anavim' in gematria, so the meraglim faced a judgment so strong they could hardly withstand it.

Like Shaul's 'hakimosi es dvar Hashem', which proved true through Purim, the delay for Miriam proved good: leaving seven days earlier would have put the meraglim's departure on Chof-Gimmel Sivan and spoiled that day of joy forever.

Every building of the Mikdash is preceded by wiping out Amalek: the Mishkan after the war with Amalek, Shaul's war on Erev Pesach that could have brought the eternal Mikdash, and Mordechai before the second Beis HaMikdash.

The two nesi'im who sinned, Elitzur ben Shdeiur and Shlumiel ben Tzurishaddai, correspond to Tamuz and Av, read in the Shabbosos of those months, and 'otzem einav me're'os bera' equals their names in gematria.
The angel of Esav's refusal to tell Yaakov his name reveals the yetzer hara's method: a name is a person's shlichus, and the yetzer hara makes people forget who sent them.

The Chasam Sofer reconciles who sent the meraglim: in that season Hashem wanted them sent with a good report, while the Satan stirred the wicked to want them too; the Mashgiach ties this to the travel of these months.

The Mashgiach reads the at-bash rule, that the first day of Pesach falls on the weekday of Tisha B'Av, as showing that Tisha B'Av is planted in the night of geulah, with the beitzah on the Seder plate as its sign.
Since Pesach assigns every festival its day, and Tisha B'Av takes its day from the first day of Pesach, Tisha B'Av is given the first seat among the Yamim Tovim, as Pesach's partner.
The months are fixed by the Sanhedrin, but the week is Hashem's own calendar; therefore the aveilus that begins with a week must first be allowed by Shabbos, the day of joy.
Tefillin are not worn on Tisha B'Av morning because one still hopes the day will become a Yom Tov, on which tefillin are not worn; only when most of the day has passed are they put on.
Since Yirmiyahu was a gilgul of Shlomo, Tisha B'Av is a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres, and the meal before it on Shabbos is like Shlomo in his time, not like Yirmiyahu.

Just as Shemini Atzeres is the ninth day of the festival in the Diaspora, Tisha B'Av is the ninth day that will become a day of simcha; the Mashgiach ties this to the Chasam Sofer's statement that a second Yom Tov will be kept after Moshiach comes.
Tu B'Av, seven days after Tisha B'Av like the end of shivah, is Tisha B'Av in a different garment: the Yom Tov of the ba'al teshuvah, and therefore greater than Pesach, the Yom Tov of the tzaddik.

Because the mitzvos work in harmony like the organs of a body, stopping to eat at Shalosh Seudos of a Shabbos that is Tisha B'Av is not Tisha B'Av intruding on Shabbos but Shabbos's own highest hour of union, which is why shoes may stay on.
Yirmiyahu's protest over buying Chanamel's field came from knowing he was Shlomo reborn: whoever hoped to shelter in his merit was relying on the one most responsible for the Churban.
Eichah ends with 'chadesh yameinu kekedem' because Yirmiyahu, remembering how good it was to write Shir HaShirim, longed to be Shlomo again.

'Each man under his vine and fig tree' describes Shlomo's era not as abundance of food but as nezirus and Shabbos, since the vine teaches the measure of the nazir and the fig the measure for carrying on Shabbos.
The verse 'atah hor'eisa lada'as' read on Tisha B'Av and brought out again at Shemini Atzeres shows that the season from Tisha B'Av to Shemini Atzeres is one transformation of Yirmiyahu into Shlomo.
Shlomo, the strongest king in the world, had no sword in his own court and had to send for one, because he conquered with wisdom and peace, as Moshiach ben David will.

The future tense of 'Yismach Hashem b'ma'asav' shows that even Hashem's joy in His creation is completed only with Moshiach; Shlomo, who attained all he wished, lived ahead of his time in that future.
Since Yirmiyahu is a gilgul of Shlomo, the day of Yirmiyahu is a hidden form of the day of Shlomo: Tisha B'Av would have been the completion of Shemini Atzeres.
The Mashgiach reads 'tzom hachamishi' with rearranged letters as 'tzom hamashiach', tying the fast of Av to Moshiach's day.
The seudah before Tisha B'Av on Shabbos is like the meal of Shlomo in his time, meaning Shlomo as he was Shlomo, not as he became Yirmiyahu.
The Mashgiach reads the Mishnah's 'go out and see King Shlomo' as a call to behold Yirmiyahu transformed back into Shlomo, wearing garments of salvation and kingship.
Reading the Shemini Atzeres maftir immediately before Yirmiyahu's first haftarah of the Three Weeks is itself a message that Tisha B'Av must be turned into Shemini Atzeres.

The Mashgiach reads the trop pair over 'alpayim ba'amah' as the two months: kanei parah, sounding like a pazer (scattering), is Av, and yerach ben yomo, its servant note, is Nisan, which supplies Av what it lacks.
He links the cow's horn being 'gildei gildei' to the kanei parah note: a segmented horn is pizur, the opposite of the shofar's achdus, and so it belongs to Av, the month of galus.

Using the kashrus concept of ben yomo, he explains the Shelah's statement that every day of Nisan is like Rosh Chodesh: Nisan is literally a 'yerach ben yomo', a month whose freshness never fades, mirroring Hashem's love that never grows stale.

He offers a reason of pshat for kashering Midian's vessels even when they are not ben yomo: Midian tried to make Hashem's ever-fresh love stale, so Hashem's hatred of Midian stays ever-fresh, and their vessels are always treated as ben yomo.
He says that shofar, spelled with the full names of its letters, equals in gematria 'kanei parah yerach ben yomo': the shofar unites the two and lets Av enjoy the blessings of Nisan.

The same soul, Betzalel then Shlomo then Yirmiyahu, built the Mishkan and the Beis HaMikdash, wrote Shir HaShirim and then Eicha, and the Mashgiach says it will again become Shlomo and sing Shir HaShirim.

'Alpayim ba'amah' is the techum Shabbos, a measure of distance; in the three weeks the pazer of scattering becomes distance from Hashem, yet under the kanei parah lies the yerach ben yomo of nearness.
The Mashgiach explains the low state of Tamuz and Av by their height: like a stone dropped from a high roof that sinks deep into soft ground, the loftier a time is, the deeper it falls.
He links the months to the tribes: Tamuz and Av correspond to Reuven and Shimon, and the falls of their nesiim, in Korach and in Pinchas, are read just as each month begins.
A summer vacation is reframed as a shlichus to repair the meraglim, who failed when they left the camp of Klal Yisrael on a journey.

Following the Chasam Sofer, the Mashgiach explains that a sender puts part of his own soul into his shliach; Hashem wanted the meraglim to go as His shluchim and succeed, but they went as shluchim of the people, whose intent was not good.
The Torah only hints that Yosef's pit held snakes and scorpions, because one may not speak ill even of a pit in Eretz Yisrael, the very sin of the meraglim.
In the Berditchever Rav's words, rushing exhausted widows for a hiddur in the matzos is putting blood into the matzos; real hiddur mitzvah is good middos.

The Mashgiach reads the naming of a parsha after Balak as a sign that his curse held the root of Moshiach, and the reading of Balak in the Three Weeks as showing that these days hide redemption within their curse.
The letters preceding those of 'anavim' hint at the power of evil, so 'the days of the first grapes' are days under its rule, yet the same words describe days in which fruit ripens.
Moshiach does not wait for all Jews to learn; he waits for the bnei Torah, the bearers of the mesorah, not to be idle.
The meraglim's sin and the jealousy over aliyos and honors in a group are one root, so overcoming that jealousy is the repair of the meraglim in these days.
Just as the top of a lulav is disqualified by a smaller flaw than the bottom, a person in a high position is more easily ruined, so not having to face such tests is itself a success.
The proof that a loud voice arouses kavanah is Ne'ilah, when in every beis medrash everyone davens aloud; the Kotzker's 'every Maariv is Kol Nidrei' teaches that this need not wait for Ne'ilah.
The two nesi'im who stumbled, one at Korach's congregation and the nasi of Shimon at Zimri's deed, correspond to the two months of Tammuz and Av, which were stricken by the sin of the meraglim.
The same pattern of Moshiach hidden under an orlah appears in soul (Balak), in place (Amon and Moav) and in time (Tammuz and Av), following the Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of world, year and soul.
Balak's inner self was good, since Moshiach was within him; it was his body, a great kelipah, that refused to let it out.
'V'hu yoshev mimuli' hints that Balak wanted to sit as the sandek and cut off the orlah of Amon and Moav, Tammuz and Av, beneath which Moshiach lies.
A bochur's especially strong yetzer hara is a sign that a great soul lies under his orlah, waiting to be revealed.
Each part of Eretz Yisrael holds a part of the Torah, so Osniel ben Kenaz's restoration of the forgotten halachos and his conquest of Kiryas Sefer were one and the same.
The souls of the last generations, 'bnei shomemah', are Tammuz-and-Av souls who struggle more and face greater trials, and so can achieve more than earlier tzaddikim.
The Mashgiach reads the doctors' white coats and the kohanim's white garments as unwitting and commanded ways of drawing down chessed, the same chessed that made the manna and an infant's milk white.

Esav's territory has a counterpart in time: the Three Weeks are Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni, the highest Shabbosos of the year, hidden because they are still Esav's province; that is why simcha may not be brought into them.
Because blessing means increase and Shabbos carries tosefes beyond its borders, Shabbos alone can cross Esav's boundary; this is why Shabbos Chazon already shows the coming consolation.

Moshe's private part of the Torah, Sefer Devarim, corresponds to his conquest of Sichon and Og: as Osniel ben Kenaz recovered halachos by conquering Kiryas Sefer, each conquest of land reveals hidden Torah.

Yerushalayim is a permanent shemittah: no one owns it, it was never divided among the tribes, and in the seventh year it extends over the whole land, a model of the future when all Eretz Yisroel becomes Yerushalayim.

Eliyahu answered Rabbah bar Avuha with Rabbi Shimon's view rather than saying he was not a kohen, because he already lives in the days of Moshiach, when all Jews are kohanim and the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon.
The three who said 'eicha', read together on Shabbos Chazon, are the shoshvinin of a wedding, making Shabbos Chazon an aufruf before the great wedding in Yerushalayim.
The Mashgiach reads the moon's name yareach as coming from rei'ach, smell: the moon is malchus and yiras shamayim, and yiras shamayim is perceived through smell, as said of Moshiach.

He explains the Sfas Emes's 'I do not smell techeiles' through this: one might prove scientifically that a dye is techeiles, but it lacks the root of yiras shamayim from the upper moon, and that is why there will be no techeiles until Moshiach.

The dor hamidbar could see a nearly full physical moon on the fourteenth and still doubt, because since the meraglim the moon one 'smells', middas malchus, was hidden from them; on Tu b'Av they sensed it again.

The upper sun and lower sun resolve both the Ramchal's question on the daily 'opening of the gates of the east' and, in the Divrei Yoel, the objection that the senses contradict Rabbeinu Tam's 72 minutes.

The moon is hidden on Rosh Hashanah because malchus must be aroused from below, through the shofar and the acceptance of malchus shamayim; Tu b'Av, as the start of that awakening, is when the moon was revealed to the dor hamidbar.

The 'deception' of the prophets was deliberate kindness: by instituting terumah and maaser outside Eretz Yisrael they made Jews feel Moshiach was near, keeping alive a hope that a revealed long exile would have crushed.
The very fact that Jews still sing Ani Maamin and await Moshiach after two thousand years shows their bond with Hashem, and is itself the sign that they must be redeemed.
Yerushalayim is read as 'yirah' and 'shalom' together, paralleling Shabbos: Friday night is the sweetness of fear of Heaven, Shabbos day is love and unity.
In these days the only valid 'passport' into Heaven is weeping and mourning, because Heaven itself is now in mourning; joy, normally the key, does not admit one now.

Because Hashem creates the world anew each moment, the burning of the Beis HaMikdash was a new fire every moment; so R' Yochanan can hold 'isho mishum chitzav' and still date the main burning to the tenth of Av.
The fire with which Hashem will rebuild Zion is the warmth of Jewish tefillos and tears, and it extinguishes the fire of sin that burned it.
Moshe's 515 prayers were in truth accepted, lacking only one more prayer, which Klal Yisrael must complete over the generations so that Moshe can enter the land with Moshiach.
Shlomo conquered the world's hearts through wisdom and fear of Heaven alone; even the sword for the judgment of the two women had to be fetched, because none was at hand.
The haftorah's claim that Shlomo completed all he desired is possible only because his reign was a taste of the days of Moshiach, raised above the limits of time.
Since time and soul correspond, Yirmiyahu being a gilgul of Shlomo means Tisha B'Av is a gilgul of Shemini Atzeres.
In an ordinary year the one who reads the maftir of Pinchas reads about Shemini Atzeres and then at once says Divrei Yirmiyahu, so that Yirmiyahu himself studies Shemini Atzeres again.
The 'Shlomo' of Moshiach's day is the seudah hamafsekes of a Shabbos erev Tisha B'Av, eaten like Shlomo's feast 'in his time', when he was still king.
The laughter of Moshiach's time is that the great tzaddikim could not bring him, while the small, lowly last generations will.
Tisha B'Av is the one moed not listed among the yomim tovim, like a bochur who could have been a yom tov but fell, and can still return.

The season itself has a bris: the Three Weeks cut off like milah, and the week from Tisha b'Av to the fifteenth of Av is its periah, so the joy of the fifteenth of Av is like the celebration when the mohel finishes.
The descendants of Keturah have milah but not periah because their bodies come from the three impure kelipos and have no part in nogah; periah, which elevates, belongs only to Yisrael.

The olah, burnt entirely, is the service of the nations, which can only renounce; the shelamim, whose meat is eaten as if on the altar, is the service of Yisrael, who can turn eating itself into avodah.

Orlah and neta revai follow the same pattern as milah and periah: three years of fruit are cut off entirely, and the fourth year's fruit is elevated in Yerushalayim, which is also where the Gemara learns brachos on food.

Metzitzah draws blood from the distant places of the body; so too after the fifteenth of Av even the bodily powers, far from Hashem, are drawn close to Him, as a preparation for crowning Him on Rosh Hashanah.
Tov v'hameitiv may only be said when another shares the good; this is why the reason of tov v'hameitiv belongs to the fifteenth of Av, the day that repairs sinas chinam.
A bachur who comes late to davening affects the angels above, since their kedushah in unison depends on Jews below saying it together.
Tu b'Av has no place in the atbash calendar sign because a sign can only be made for something that has already happened, while Tu b'Av is a festival of what will be.
Like a child who gives six excuses, the Gemara's very listing of six reasons, none sufficient alone, reveals that the true reason for Tu b'Av is still unknown.
The slain of Beitar who did not decay show that the hope for Moshiach, even when attached to a false Moshiach, is a living force, and a living thing does not decay.
The borrowed white garments of Tu b'Av hint that a Jew may borrow now from the good person he will become.
The pointing finger of the future dance of the tzaddikim conveys what words cannot: the depth of a Jewish heart that keeps hoping after so many disappointments.
The Shulchan Aruch's calendar sign leaves out the seventh day of Pesach because the festival it fixes, the Fifteenth of Av, celebrates an event that has not yet happened.
A holy event shines before it happens: as Avraham ate matzos before the Exodus, the six joys of the Fifteenth of Av were glimmers of the future redemption.
Bnos Tzelofchad grasped what Moshe Rabbeinu did not, because the share in the land means a share in Olam Haba, which is grasped with the heart rather than the intellect.
Yirmiyahu's curse on his birthday was a statement of fact, since he was born on Tisha B'Av; yet that same day is the birthday of Moshiach, so Yirmiyahu will one day bless it.
Yirmiyahu writing Eichah is Shlomo, the author of Shir HaShirim, in black garments, and 'renew our days as of old' is his plea to become Shlomo again.
When Shlomo judged the two women no sword was found among his soldiers, a sign that he ruled the world through Torah and peace, not weapons.

Jews themselves are festivals: a talmid chacham is Shabbos, who gives to the weekday Jews rather than receiving from them, and a gifted person who wastes his life is 'Reb Tisha B'Av', a mo'ed lying in the grave.

The 'shidduch' of Chamishah Asar b'Av is between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, and the tenaim one must look over before the match are the passuk of parshas Eikev: to fear Hashem, walk in His ways and love Him.
Since teshuvah begins on Chamishah Asar b'Av and ends on Yom Kippur, and the end is embedded in the beginning, the good choice a Jew has on Yom Kippur is already present on Chamishah Asar b'Av.
Yerushalayim is 'yirah shleimah': holy fear of Hashem flows from wholeness, unlike ordinary fear, which comes from a person's lack, as one fears a lion because he lacks its strength.

Tisha b'Av contains two opposites, the churban and the gain that our avodah became more precious; the gain cannot be celebrated on Tisha b'Av itself, so Chamishah Asar b'Av, when the mourning ends, was set as its yom tov.

Because 'every generation in whose days the Beis Hamikdash is not rebuilt' suffers a new churban, each year's avodah is more precious than the last, which is why the Gemara says to add in learning from Chamishah Asar b'Av.

On Shavuos the Aseres HaDibros are read because it is the fiftieth day of Sefirah, but on Shabbos Yisro they are read because of the Shabbos, so that Shabbos Yisro may be an even more powerful acceptance of the Torah than Shavuos.

Rashi's question of what Yisro heard is answered by two stories of latecomers, Dasan and Aviram at the sea and the Bnei Dan outside the clouds, from which Yisro learned that he too, though late, would be welcomed.
Hashem had to rebuke the sea because its original condition from creation had already been fulfilled; splitting a second time for Dasan and Aviram was outside that condition.
Hashem's war against Amalek in every generation stems from Amalek's attack on His children who were late and outside the clouds; nearly four thousand years later His anger still burns over it.

The Masorah's sign for the count of Yisro, Yanadav, alludes to the Rambam's one whose spirit volunteers, and the discrepancy between 72 and 75 itself shows that Torah, like the Kodesh HaKodashim, stands above arithmetic.
Just as the Torah given on the fifty-first day is still counted as the fiftieth, a person who takes on the yoke of Torah is not subject to the calculations of income and expenses.
A Yom Tov is drawn not only from its date but from the parsha that describes it: since the world was made from the Torah, reading a parsha reaches the source from which the calendar itself flows.
Yisro is greater than Rus because Shavuos belongs to the calendar, which Klal Yisrael sets, while Shabbos Yisro belongs to the Torah and to Shabbos, which Hashem gives without our effort.
The haftarah of Yisro opens with Uziyahu's tzara'as, the greatest tumah of a living person, to show that on this Shabbos the Torah is given even against a background of tumah and without preparation.
Parshas Yisro is to the Torah what the Aron was to the Kodesh HaKodashim: as the place of the Aron was not measured, the parsha that holds the Aseres HaDibros is not bound by its count of pesukim.
A dedicated talmid chacham is a third form of the Aseres HaDibros, after the Luchos in the Kodesh HaKodashim and the pesukim in Parshas Yisro, so his parnassah, like the manna, is beyond the numbers.

According to the Ba'al Shem Tov as the Mashgiach brings him, those who followed Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai and failed had imitated the style without the dveikus and love of Torah that bring the guarantee.
Shemini Atzeres, the most spiritual day of the year, is when Klal Yisrael asks for Geshem, because what they truly ask for is the inner side of the rain, a flow of Torah.
The Mabul and Matan Torah are the same forty days of water: the generation that refused the Torah received its outside as a flood, while Klal Yisrael received its inside.

Noach was the neshamah of Moshe, meant to give the Torah; failing because he did not daven for his generation, he was 'replanted' like a sapling as Moshe, who davened with mesirus nefesh and repaired the sin of 'mei Noach'.
'Bashalom' at the end of the psalm hints to the shin, the letter of Torah, so the verse describes the Torah coming down as water; the Mashgiach adds that it drizzled at Matan Torah.
Oil, which makes no noise when spilled, is linked to eight, above the seven days of creation, while wine, numerically seventy, belongs to the seven.
The ayalah that can give birth only when the snake strikes her is Klal Yisrael: the suffering of galus, especially the chevlei Moshiach, is the very agent that will deliver the days of Moshiach.

The Mashgiach reads the count of Bamidbar, on the Shabbos before Shavuos, as the aufruf of the kallah: counting the Jews is counting the letters of the Torah, and that is adorning the kallah before the wedding.
Amen joins the written Name, Havaya (26), with the spoken Name, Adnus (65), making 91, because we perceive Hashem only through His Shechinah dwelling on Klal Yisrael, the kallah.
A Jew's face carries the aleph: the two eyes are its two yuds and the nose its vav, together the Shem Havaya, and the mouth below is the patach of chochmah.
Numbers erase individuality: the Nazis tattooed numbers on Jews to make them like branded animals, while Hashem counts 'by names', each Jew a distinct shlichus with no duplicates.
Shevet Levi is the root of the 600,000 letters, the 22 letters of the alef-beis, which is why the Levi'im numbered 22,000, and this resolves 600,000 versus 22,000 malachim at Sinai.
Staying up Shavuos night and sleeping through the davening is like a chassan who pays for everything but skips the ring: without it there is no wedding.
The Mashgiach reads shifcha as mishpacha missing its mem: the Eved Ivri who becomes permitted to a shifcha has lost the mem, the forty days of Matan Torah that made Klal Yisrael a family.
Shavuos, the fiftieth day, is a miniature Yovel, the fiftieth year: the great shofar at Sinai parallels the shofar of Yovel that frees the slave and returns each man to his portion.

The camps in the wilderness mirror the Chumash: four camps around the center for five Chumashim, with Vayikra, about the Mishkan, Kohanim and Levi'im, in the middle; so each Jew stood in the camp exactly where his letter is.
The Mashgiach explains the extraordinary heresy of our time by the generation's mitzvah being emunah: what a person or generation is rooted in is exactly where he must struggle.
The last seven letters of the Aseres Hadibros, 'asher lerei'echa', correspond to the seven rabbinic mitzvos, since the true friends who seek our welfare are the Chachamim.
Rus and Yisro, both read on Shavuos, are built of the same letters, Yisro being Rus with an extra yud, because both embody the soul's return to its source.
A year is called shanah because it means repetition: whatever happened on a Yom Tov repeats itself each year, so Matan Torah truly recurs every Shavuos.
The Mashgiach describes Shabbos as a rope thrown to the eved to return, and Yovel as the lifeguard who pulls him out by the hair when he will not grab it; the shofar of Moshiach will do the same.
The Mashgiach says he is convinced, though he has not seen it in a sefer, that the place of Yovel is Beis Lechem Yehudah, the home of David HaMelech, whose malchus gathers Jews back.
Boaz's 'dip your bread in vinegar' becomes a blessing: her bread will be dipped in the halacha that Menashe taught about how to make hamotzi.
The Mishnah and the Gemara on Menashe's share are both true at different levels, just as a deeper level of judgment in Eretz Yisrael can reopen a case closed abroad.
Yibum itself is Hashem's tunnel under the Kisei HaKavod: hard work digging to bring a lost soul to its tikkun, which is why it belongs to Moshiach.

Baking is the last stage in the tikkun of a soul in bread, so the part baked first shows that Hashem is hurrying its tikkun; that is why the bracha is made there, and why Menashe of malchus Beis David taught it.
Shabbos is a return one may decline, like the eved who chooses to stay at Shemitah, but Yom Kippur and Yovel pull a person out by force, so Yovel is the return that is for everyone.
In the Ramak's fiftieth mention of yetzias Mitzrayim the Torah says 'I took them out' in the third person, because the fiftieth level is hidden and beyond us.
After the forty-nine klalos in groups of seven, the fiftieth mention comes, showing that the sitra achra has a grip on forty-nine levels but not on the fiftieth.
The kedushah of Yosef and Serach protected every Jew in Mitzrayim up to, but not including, the fiftieth level, and Shlomis's son needed exactly that level, so she stumbled.
Rus is said to 'return' from Moav though she had never been in Eretz Yisrael, because her neshamah belonged there; Beis Lechem, where Rachel is, corresponds to the mitzvah of Yovel.
The fifty thousand Yovlos the Mashgiach heard are not a measure of time but of levels: the tikkun of the lowest requires a level made of fifty thousand Yovlos.

The Mashgiach reads the modern idea of freedom, doing whatever one wants, as the very slavery the Torah frees a Jew from: the smoker who claims freedom is enslaved to his yetzer hara, while the free man is one who chooses to serve Hashem.
He links the fiftieth year of Yovel with the fiftieth day of Sefirah: both are freedom and return, going out from being a slave to the yetzer hara to being a servant of Hashem.
The year is like a rotating card file: each day carries what happened on it, so a Yom Tov is a real return of the original event and not a commemoration like the Fourth of July.
He explains why the parsha of the Yamim Tovim in Emor begins with Shabbos, which is not one of them: each Yom Tov draws its blessing from the Shabbos before it.

The twenty-four books of Tanach said on Shavuos night are the twenty-four ornaments of the kallah, paralleled by the twenty-four permutations of the four letters of the Name of Adnus, which represents the kallah.
He offers a simple reading of a Midrash Peliah: Shavuos is a time to become a Jew anew, as Yisro and Rus did, and as the Yid HaKadosh did every day.

The Mashgiach presents Yovel as a law of nature like gravity: just as an apple must fall back to the ground it came from, every Yid must eventually return to his source in Eretz Yisrael and in Hashem.

The difference between the seventh year and Yovel is that in the seventh year Hashem throws the drowning slave a rope that he can refuse, while at Yovel He dives in like a lifeguard and pulls him out by the hair.
The fifty days from Mitzrayim to Matan Torah parallel the fifty years of Yovel, so that the shofar at Sinai is the shofar of freedom calling the Yidden back to their roots.
Since the chance of Moshiach coming is even every day, like a spinning penny that does not remember its past throws, two thousand years of waiting do not lessen the chance that he comes this Shavuos.
The teshuvah the Yidden did on arriving at Sinai returns every Rosh Chodesh Sivan, and the Torah demands preparation only for Shavuos, not for Pesach or Sukkos.
The Mashgiach reads the eved Ivri who refuses to leave as a picture of a person who prefers his chains, and the Yovel shofar as a holiness of freedom that descends and makes even him want to go free.
Sefiras ha'omer mirrors Shemitah and Yovel: seven times seven, with the fiftieth day corresponding to the fiftieth year, so the shofar at Har Sinai is the Yovel shofar of the Jewish people.

The smoker who says one cigarette cannot shorten his life is refuted by simple arithmetic: ten thousand cigarettes are ten thousand times one cigarette, so each one shortens it, and his laughter shows he is kidding himself.
Akdamus, said with the Sefer Torah already on the bimah, is understood as a last stage of preparation, a lesson in emunah before hearing the Aseres Hadibros.
Shavuos differs from the Fourth of July: nothing happens on Independence Day besides remembering, while on Shavuos the Torah is actually given again, a whole year's supply.
The Sanzer Rav's answer shows that being shown a spiritual vision is little; the goal is to grow until one can see it with his own strength.
Unlike a secular holiday that recalls a past event, a Jewish yom tov brings down again the very lights of the original event, so each Jew stands at Sinai every Shavuos.
Even one who does not hear the thunder of Sinai must believe, as the Kotzker taught, that believing is greater than seeing, and that his soul hears it.
Shavuos is a judgment more fearsome than Rosh Hashanah, for on it one's portion in Torah and in heartfelt davening is decided, not only bread and milk.
The all-night learning is like the wedding's music and flowers; the davening and the Ten Commandments are the ring and the chuppah, without which nothing has happened.
Listening to krias haTorah is Torah lishmah precisely because one learns nothing new from it, and on Shavuos it includes all 613 mitzvos within the Ten Commandments.
From 'Moshe yedaber' in the future tense the Mashgiach learns that Moshe speaks with each Jew every Shavuos, not only at the original Matan Torah.
Mesiras nefesh means giving over one's will, since 'nefesh' means will, as in 'im yesh es nafshechem'.
Shavuos is a greater day of judgment than Rosh Hashanah, because Rosh Hashanah judges material matters while Shavuos decides the spiritual life of the coming year.
Calling a person to the Torah by his name and his father's name mirrors Moshe's counting 'by their families and fathers' houses', binding him to his root letter.
The fiftieth day is not counted and Shavuos has no fixed calendar date because it is the root, above time and number, just as the Levi'im, the camp of the Shechinah, are not counted.
The four camps correspond to four books of the Chumash, with Vayikra, the book of the Kohanim and Levi'im, in the middle like the camp of the Shechinah.
The days of sefirah prepare the body as parchment, rubbing and smoothing it so that Hashem's Sefer Torah can be written on each Jew.

The Ten Commandments are counted by the Masorah as ten parshiyos rather than thirteen pesukim, which is why it gives 72 pesukim for Yisro; the Mashgiach calls this a strained answer that is nevertheless true.
The 'mistake' in the count of Parshas Yisro is itself the lesson: the place of the luchos, like the Aron that occupied no space, is not subject to arithmetic.
The fiftieth day of sefirah is not counted because it is a heavenly day beyond the fifty gates, on which Hashem brought heaven down to Har Sinai.

The levels of talmidei chachamim parallel the holy days: one who does nothing but learn is like Shabbos, one who works only for food is like Yom Tov, and lesser levels are like Chol HaMoed and Rosh Chodesh.
The Masorah's sign for the 72 pesukim of Yisro, 'v'Nadav', hints at the Rambam's words about one whose spirit moves him to give himself to Hashem.
Yisro was moved specifically by the war with Amalek because Amalek attacked the latecomers, and Hashem's anger at that showed Yisro that a latecomer is still precious to Hashem.

The Magen Avraham's question how the sixth of Sivan can be called 'the day of the giving of our Torah' is answered simply: the Torah is given anew each Shavuos, so this year's Shavuos is truly that day.
The Jews reached Sinai on Rosh Chodesh because the moon's renewal renews the 'crops' of every Jew's soul, which grow from the moon, making it the time for new kabbalos.
Through Rabbi Gedalia Chayun, a convert's every later mitzvah is 'compounded' with the mitzvah of her conversion, because without that acceptance she would never have done it.
The world did not wait for the giving of the Torah but for the Jews' acceptance of it, as the Gemara's 'one of your eyes' refers to the moment of acceptance before fulfillment.

Rashi's 'wherever it says neged, it means facing east' becomes a call to keep all of life turned toward one point, the glorification of Hashem, rising like the dawn, without being scattered by obstacles or by looking back.
The world's apathy in the face of danger is described as a disease, a failure to notice what is happening.
Naomi is the Shechinah going down into Moav, the territory of the sitra achra, to rescue the spark from which David and Moshiach will come; the famine and Elimelech's departure served this purpose.

The disorder before Moshiach is like a bone thrown to a dog: just as the Satan was sent to Iyov so he would not obstruct the splitting of the sea, the lower forces of evil are given something to occupy them so they will not disturb the preparation of Moshiach.
The Mashgiach reads 'Your right hand, Hashem, shatters the enemy' as alluding to Iyov, since oyev and Iyov share the same letters.

Chazal read immodesty into the verses of Rus but not into the maidens of Shaul's time, because the signs of ikvesa d'Meshicha belonged to the time when the spark of Moshiach was being born, not to David's settled generation.
Chutzpah serves as the camouflage of Moshiach's coming: the line of Moshiach began with the brazen naming of Moav, and 'chutzpah will increase' is the first sign listed in the Baraisa.
Rus is placed right after Malachi because Malachi's closing describes the torn generations before Eliyahu comes, and that is exactly the state of 'the days when the judges were judged'.
Rus's complete reward was to live to see Shlomo's kingship, a time when converts are not accepted, because she converted when being a Jew was hard and could then see how good it is to be a Jew.
The world is called olam because it hides its Creator; on Shavuos, the fiftieth day that is beyond counting, the hidden things begin to be revealed.
The angels' taking permission from one another teaches that no one should push himself forward; each one's song only counts as part of the whole choir.
The truest song is what remains unsaid: each Jew's private grasp of Hashem, which he cannot explain even to others, is the 'secret of the Torah'.
Even the simplest Jew has a point in his soul through which he knows Hashem more deeply than the greatest tzaddik.
The angels long all their existence for one chance to sing, while a Jew has that chance every minute of his life.
Each accepted prayer of a Jew becomes a precious stone in Hashem's crown, set opposite His tefillin, and on Shavuos this crown is revealed.
The holier a thing is, the more easily it is affected; therefore Olam Haba was hidden even from the prophets.
The Midrash says 'zman' for the earlier turning points but 'eis' for Matan Torah, because 'eis' (related to 'atah', now) is a dimensionless point between past and future, and the Torah is above time.
Although the Torah says to count fifty days, the count ends at forty-nine: the fiftieth day, like Yovel and Yom Kippur, belongs to a level above time that a person cannot count.
The chametz of the two loaves is the refined 'chametz of the future', a yetzer hara made holy, so on the day of the Torah one brings a new kind of service to Hashem from chametz.

The counting runs from chesed down to malchus because the Avos and Moshe brought the Shechinah down from the seventh heaven step by step, and every person is meant to become a Har Sinai on which Heaven descends.
For a tzaddik, what is beyond the letter of the law for others becomes his law, and 'kedoshim tihyu' means that yesterday's extra becomes today's baseline.

The son's question 'tomorrow' is the question of the morning after the Seder, when the elevation is gone; the strong hand of Pesach is not the purpose, since man was created to sanctify himself by his own work.

The hagbalah at Sinai, being told to stay below, is not the opposite of preparing for Torah but the preparation itself: knowing one is limited and unworthy readies a person to receive the Torah as a gift.

The verse of the last week of sefirah is "afsei aretz", the ends of the earth: one who began sefirah with great hopes ends at the lowest point, and from there, with the cry "shavaseinu kabel", he comes to receive the Torah.

Megillas Ruth is read on Shavuos because Torah and tefillah go together: Ruth is the root of Dovid, the pillar of tefillah, and the megillah's opening about ten famines points to the last famine, for the word of Hashem, which only prayer can break.

The Targum repeats at the end of Ruth what it said at the start, that Boaz ended the famine through prayer, because the megillah is a psak written by Shmuel on Dovid's lineage, and a psak restates its reason at the end.
Ruth and Orpah both accepted the yoke of Heaven; the only difference was that Ruth's acceptance stayed fresh, and that small difference produced Dovid on one side and Golias on the other.
Following Tosafos, what disqualified a ba'al keri before Matan Torah was not tumah, which did not yet exist, but kalus rosh, the opposite of the awe with which Torah must be received.
Staying up on Shavuos night with toil in Torah repairs the acceptance of the Oral Torah, which according to Midrash Tanchuma was not accepted willingly at Sinai.

The Mashgiach reads the word 'shanah' (year) as coming from 'shinui', repetition: the year is like a rotating card file, and when a day's card comes down to the lower world, what happened on that date happens again.

Like a patient under anesthetic at the dentist, a coarse person may feel nothing at Matan Torah, yet the procedure is real: his soul receives the lights of Matan Torah and carries them through the year.
Unlike every other Yom Tov, named for what happens on it, Shavuos is named for the counting of the weeks before it, showing how essential the preparation is.
A mikveh, like a sukkah, is not its water or its boards and straw but the holy names that its halachos draw into it; the mikveh of Shavuos carries different holy names than during the year.

Staying up all night and sleeping through Krias HaTorah is like a chassan who paid for the caterer, photographers and flowers but came to the chuppah without the ring, since Israel is the chassan and the Torah the kallah.
Rosh Chodesh Sivan, the head of the month, already contains all of Shavuos, as Rosh Hashanah contains the whole year.

A tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah can rule over heavenly ministers without knowing it himself, as the Mishneh LaMelech's shake of the head cast down the minister of Russia while only the Ba'al Shem Tov knew.

The rule that the lower prevails explains both the order of meat and milk and the dispute at Sinai: the angels held the upper prevails, so the Torah should stay in heaven, and by their own rule their meal at Avraham's table was meat with milk.
Milk on Shavuos reflects the transformation of din into chesed: as blood becomes milk, the red days of sefirah become white.
A Sefer Torah is written on an animal's hide to show that the Torah's letters must rest on the person's refined animal side, made clean and white.

The camp of Israel in the wilderness was a living Sefer Torah, so a person who did not belong in a camp was like an extra letter that invalidates the scroll; this, not exclusion, is why the blasphemer was kept out.
The Levi'im were counted from thirty days old, the start of a person's root, because they are the roots of the letters, matching the 22 letters as 22,000.
The commandments were said in the singular so that even in a guilty generation the Torah endures through individuals, whose worth then is like that of Adam, created alone.
Unlike the nations, who merely commemorate a past event on its date, for Jews the same lights of the original day actually return each year, which is why a year is called shanah, repetition.
Every soul relives matan Torah each Shavuos; a sin is like the insulation on an electric wire, which keeps the body from feeling the current the soul experiences.
On Rosh Hashanah one is judged for parnassah, but on Shavuos one is judged for one's share in Torah and closeness to Hashem, so Shavuos calls for even more fear.
The one who stays awake all night and then sleeps at the Aseres Hadibros is like a chasan who paid for the hall, music and flowers but will not buy the ring, without which there is no kiddushin.

Just as physical air and rivers are polluted today, so is the spiritual atmosphere, following the principle that one can recognize the state of ruchniyus from gashmiyus; for that reason a struggling Jew's avodah is worth more now.

The left horn of Yitzchak's ram was already sounded at Sinai, and the right horn remains for Moshiach; the Torah comes from Hashem's right hand, so Kabbalas HaTorah is a time to arouse that right side in mercy.

The Mashgiach pairs the two Gemara statements with the two days: Yom Kippur, the atonement of the golden calf, teaches teshuvah for the many, while Hoshana Rabbah, Dovid's day, teaches teshuvah for the individual.
The 'individual' is the Jew who cannot be included in the klal because of a barrier; this is why the Hoshana Rabbah aravah is taken apart from the lulav bundle that binds all Jews together.
The hoshana beaten on the ground, lowered to the dust, is then raised to become a crown on the aron kodesh, an image of 'mekimi me'afar dal' and of Dovid HaMelech.
The seventy nations fought on Sukkos are in truth the spiritual forces of the yetzer hara that can enter a Jewish heart.

Just as Hashem guards the hidden point of emunah inherited from Avraham (Magen Avraham), He guards the point of tefillah each Jew has from Dovid (Magen Dovid), so that even in his lowest state a Jew can pour out his heart.
'Every man in debt' among Dovid's men includes the Jew who does not even know he owes a debt to Hashem; such people too enlist with Dovid.
Moshiach is called poor not because he lacks anything of his own but because he lacks us: his poverty is his longing for Klal Yisrael.
Since the great kehillos of earlier generations did not bring Moshiach with their teshuvah, the promise of 'one kehillah' must be fulfilled by a humble kehillah of our own time.
In the deep hester panim of today, every small movement of a kehillah toward Hashem is worth as much as the great avodos of earlier generations.

'Lo se'ametz es levavcha' is read as a call not to harden one's heart to the longing of Moshiach and the Shechinah, since through people fulfilling Hashem's will Moshiach is given the strength to bring the tikkun.
Saying Dovid's songs in Pesukei Dezimra and Hallel makes Jews, as it were, Dovid HaMelech's minyan: he says them and we say them together with him.
The aravah, which has neither taste nor smell, is the present generation, and Tehillim's 'He turned to the prayer of the destitute' was written for that last generation.
Dovid is the esrog, the most beautiful of the species, yet on Hoshana Rabbah he lowers himself to the aravah, the lowest, to accept the prayer of the destitute.
The events reported in the news from the war are only a reflection of the battle fought in the shul.
Pesukei dezimra are a weapon because they cut down the klipos, and the seven hakafos on the seventh day bring down the walls as at Yericho.
When Jews say Dovid's songs with intent and outpouring of the soul, they arouse Dovid himself to daven together with them.
The aravah's lack of taste and smell, its emptiness, is exactly what makes it the mitzvah of the day of Dovid, whose malchus is to have nothing of his own.
The largest treasury, that of free gifts, is not reached by everyone because it only opens for one who truly feels he deserves nothing and has no claim on Hashem.
Dovid said not 'I pray' but 'I am tefillah': like a poor man in rags whose appearance needs no explanation, his very state was his request.
The lowly state of today's generation, compared with the tearful avodah of earlier simple Jews, can itself become its tefillah, as in 'va'ani tefillah'.
All the Yamim Tovim circle around Shemini Atzeres, which is not itself a 'chag' but the center point where Hashem stands, and Hoshana Rabbah's higher teshuvah is the preparation to enter it.

The Mashgiach distinguishes two wars of Gog and Magog: a physical one with the nations that will come with Moshiach, and a spiritual one against the ministers of the nations, against emunah and the handing down of Torah, which is already burning now.

He links the seven Canaanite nations to the seven middos and, in general, to the seventy nations, and the seven days of circling the bimah to the seven days around Yericho, whose fallen wall is the yetzer hara that separates a Jew from Hashem.

The three kinds of men in Dovid's army, the pressed, the debtor and the bitter of soul, describe every Jew today, who is in debt to Hashem through his sins; precisely this qualifies him for Dovid's army.

Following the Chiddushei HaRim, the Mashgiach reads 've'ein moshia lah' as pointing to the level of 'ayin', a level above measure where the accusers have no entry, so crying out reaches a place they cannot block.

The aravah, which has neither taste nor smell, is held after setting aside the other species, and beating it on the ground expresses that a Jew comes before Hashem with nothing but his lowliness, which is what brings the chasimah.
Hoshana Rabbah is the day of tefillah, while Shemini Atzeres and Simchas Torah are already Torah, so the day's success is taking tefillah on oneself for the whole year.
The aravah, which has neither taste nor smell, is the tefillah of Dovid HaMelech: prayer is open to the lowliest Jew, and on Hoshana Rabbah the aravah takes the most important place after Hallel.
Moshe's tefillos were in fact accepted: they completed the roof of the heavenly Mikdash, so the lesson to daven in a time of trouble is learned from an answered prayer, not an unanswered one.

Shiloh's roof was of curtains, and the roofs of the first two Batei Mikdash were unsanctified, because the roof corresponds to keser, which can rest only in Yerushalayim and only once Amalek, gematria ram, is gone.
Before every Mikdash there was a war with Amalek, by Yehoshua, Shaul and Mordechai, but none was a full victory, which is why each Mikdash fell short of the Mikdash above.

Rabban Gamliel's beracha against the heretics is the only one whose Name is pointed with a kamatz, corresponding to keser; it was needed only after the Churban, and this may be the hidden meaning of the child's translation in Lublin.
Moshe built the fifth camp with 515 tefillos, five times machaneh; Moshiach with his camp will be the sixth, which brings the Mikdash with its holy roof down to this world.

The 515 hours from Rosh Hashanah until the last hour of Shemini Atzeres morning match Moshe's 515 tefillos, so his prayer was a Hoshana Rabbah prayer, and the missing last hour is left for later generations to daven.
Shemini Atzeres is not called 'chag' because 'chag' means going around in a circle, while Shemini Atzeres is the point in the middle, where one can point and say 'this is our G-d'.
Just as the aravah, last mitzvah of Sukkos, stands for the lips, casting it away marks the move to a day that can no longer be put into words.

Torah is always tied to the eighth: it was given at the start of the eighth week of the Sefirah, and in Tehillim 19 seven verses speak of nature while the eighth, 'Toras Hashem temimah', is above nature.
Shlomo sending the people away on the eighth day hints that the King of kings sends the nations home with their gifts, while His children run after Him into the palace.
Tefillas geshem is said in the blessing of techiyas hameisim to teach that one must not be lifeless: learning, davening and mitzvos must all be done with vitality.

The Sefer Torah is read from the beginning again because all Jews, each a letter in it, form a circle around Hashem in the middle, as the Gemara at the end of Taanis describes the circle of tzaddikim.

Because the generations keep shrinking, the Zohar's promise of a kenishta chada that brings the geulah must be fulfilled by a later generation, whose small turning to Hashem is worth more than much of the earlier generations' service.
Mourning for Yerushalayim is not only a sign of loss but the first step of its rebuilding, which is why the building of the kallah begins on Tisha B'Av.
The reading cycle of Devarim, from Shabbos Chazon to Simchas Torah, matches the building of the kallah from Tisha B'Av to Shemini Atzeres, since Devarim is the seventh book and the kallah.
The esrog is held apart from the bound lulav, and Devarim alone does not begin with a vav, because the kallah must first be separate, like Chavah from Adam, so that their reunion brings joy.
Shir Hashirim praises the kallah from the feet up because the lowest generations are the most precious to Hashem, and the last generation is the true beauty of Knesses Yisroel.
Shimshon's strength lay in his hair because hair is the last thing formed in a person, the aspect of Dan and of acharis, and the last generation must likewise not let itself be shorn.

On Simchas Torah one rejoices at the end of the Torah, the place of forgotten halachos and of the forgotten Jews of the last generations, because it is joined at once to Bereishis, so every Jew will have a tikkun.

Sitting in real huts at war would have been no reminder of war at all, since a soldier's way is to hide in trenches; the huts show instead that the protection of the Clouds of Glory went out with the Jews.
Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva do not disagree about the miracle at all; according to both the Clouds of Glory protected the Jews, which removes the difficulty with the Shulchan Aruch and the Bach.
If the protection could leave the camp and go with the soldiers from place to place, it can also go from time to time; this is how 'so that your generations will know' reaches every generation.
The second half of the passuk, 'all the citizens in Israel shall dwell in sukkos', refers to the whole year: a Jew living in his apartment is still dwelling in the sukkah that went along with him.
When Moshe wrote 'vayamos sham Moshe' while still alive, he gave his soul into the Torah, so that his passing lies in those words; in the same way a passuk can carry the life of a day.

Comfort as a condition of a mitzvah appears only where the mitzvah is itself a physical act made holy, like eating, dwelling in Eretz Yisrael or dwelling in the sukkah; there suffering means the mitzvah is not being done at all.
The tzaddikim who stayed in the sukkah in the rain did not override the exemption of one who suffers; leaving would have made them suffer more, so for them the halachah itself required staying.
Rashi's 'so as not to trouble him with guests' is turned around: Hashem saw that the heat did not trouble Avraham at all, but the lack of guests did, so He sent guests.

Rabbi Zeira reads 'a shelter from storm and rain' as the sukkah's own nature: a sukkah kept in perfection, like the Clouds of Glory, keeps out the rain, so the Ba'al Shem Tov's dry sukkah was the mitzvah in its completeness, not a miracle.
Under every forced reading of Tosafos lies something hidden, like a bulge under a fine tablecloth that hides an ornament rather than a craftsman's mistake.

The angels were damaged by Sodom's impurity just as an angel would have been by Egypt's; their repair had to come through Yaakov, who did the opposite and grew greater in the place of greatest impurity.
The angels were the fitting messengers to Esav because they were the living witnesses that Yaakov had not been damaged at Lavan's, since their own repair depended on it.
The Torah's repetition of 'in the seventh month' is a demand to go against nature: exactly when everything withers, a Jew is to take living species and stay fresh.
The esrog is taken first because it is the one exception in nature that does not dry out in winter; it can pass through all the seasons and remain alive.

The dispute between the Mechaber and the Rema over a split middle leaf rests on whether the top leaf is a separate leaf or a seamless continuation of the spine; if it is the spine, even a fully split leaf is still only a minority of the spine, so 'most of it is like all of it' does not apply.
The leaves of the lulav are the parts of the year, and its head is the head of the year, the period from Rosh Hashanah to Shemini Atzeres; if the head is dried out, the whole year suffers.
The special joy of Sukkos is freshness itself, the opposite of drowsiness, as shown by those who did not sleep at Simchas Beis Hashoeva.
The sukkah is a measure of Yerushalayim confined within its walls, while Shemini Atzeres is higher: its Yerushalayim breaks through the walls and spreads to the whole world.
The sukkah is the 'Hashem around His people' of Tehillim: a Yerushalayim whose surrounding wall is Hashem Himself, which no enemy can breach, unlike the physical mountains around the city.

Shem's reward for covering his father with zeal was living mekifim like the sukkah, the mitzvah of life, while Yefes, who only followed along, received 'dead' mekifim, the burial of Gog read about in the Sukkos haftarah.
The many requests of Shemoneh Esrei do not contradict the rule to pray for one thing, since every lack, of mind, health or peace, is a lack in the one request to serve Hashem with a settled mind.
The water of the simchas beis hashoevah is only a physical envelope for ruach hakodesh; the celebration is named after the drawing because simcha is the bucket that draws it.

Only Sukkos is called 'seven days in the year', because what is drawn in these seven days enters the whole year; sleeping through them would mean sleeping away a whole year, as Moshe could not sleep on the mountain knowing what each minute held.

The ruach hakodesh of Sukkos is the 'speaking spirit' of Onkelos: after Yom Kippur a Jew is like a newborn, and just as a father teaches Torah to a child who begins to talk, Hashem teaches him to speak, culminating in Simchas Torah.
Ruach hakodesh does not mean knowing which number will win a sweepstakes; it means speaking true words of Torah and tefillah, a level open to every Jew according to his level.
The Mashgiach reads the joy of Simchas Beis Hashoevah as the joy of the water itself, returning to its root, with the Jews rejoicing together with the water.
He parallels the Foundation Stone, the root of place from which the world was founded, with Tishrei, the root of time, hinted in the letters of Bereishis.
Since the libation is halachah given to Moshe at Sinai and Torah cannot be destroyed, the libation continues in a hidden way even after the destruction, and the waters still have their ascent.
The place from which the waters return to Hashem, the shafts beneath the altar, is the same place from which Jewish souls come, since Adam was created from the earth of the altar.
Dancing is a leap toward heaven: one cannot touch the sky, but the jump shows the will to be there, which is why the Mishnah mentions dancing only at Simchas Beis Hashoevah.
Science can explain how the waves rise but not why nature was made so; the sefarim say the waves rise out of longing to be near the King, knowing they will not reach Him.

The Mashgiach reasons that Sukkos, coming after Pesach and Shavuos, cannot share Pesach's level of emunah; the 'shade of emunah' must be higher than the 'food of emunah', and he identifies it as bitachon, which alone brings simcha.
Commemorating the clouds of glory rather than the well or the manna is explained by the clouds containing every need, so the sukkah itself carries the blessing of parnassah.

A gift is a sign of mission: Navos's sweet voice showed his task was song, and the vineyard, whose wine is the vehicle of song, was given him for that task, so when he stopped singing both the vineyard and his life were taken.

Achav's desire for the vineyard was a true pull toward sparks of his own soul; by law the vineyard would have reached him anyway, and his sin was in not waiting, yet the vineyard still brought him to teshuvah.

The closing words of Melachim, 'from the king' without 'of Bavel', reflect revealed providence: Yehoyachin, a tzaddik, knew his bread came from Hashem, while Yirmiyahu, the book of the churban, records how it looked under hidden providence.
The 'flood' the nations feared at Matan Torah was a flood of Torah; likewise the danger feared in the coming year can be turned into blessing by Jews who accept the Torah.

The Mashgiach explains Samael's 'mistake' as flight, not ignorance: he knows Betzer is the city of refuge, but Betzer, Moshe's city and the place of Moshiach's mitzvah, smells of Moshiach, so he cannot bear to stay there.
According to the Mashgiach, Moshiach is called chasan Torah because he completes the keeping of the Torah through the three added cities of refuge, the only mitzvah still missing.

He shows that 'ויספת לך עוד שלש' equals in gematria the mitzvah of appointing a king, and that 'אז יבדיל משה שלש ערים' likewise matches it, so the cities of refuge are the king's mitzvah, begun by Moshe and finished by Moshiach.

The Mashgiach explains that kingship is not native to Israel and had to be imported from Moav, which is gematria 49, malchus shebemalchus; David is the holy spark freed from Moav's klipah, and 'ומחץ פאתי מואב' is his breaking it.
He reads Yishmael's name as a promise: because his exile is the bitterest, Hashem will hear the prayers of Jews in it, and a prayer that reaches the Thirteen Attributes is accepted.
The Mashgiach explains that the final seal can come after Yom Kippur because the sukkah has the quality of Eretz Yisrael, where a fugitive's sentence is reopened for the land's merit.
From the Mishnah of the sea creature that flees to land, the Mashgiach learns that where a creature runs in danger shows its root, and a Jew in distress runs to Hashem, the sukkah and the Torah.

The Torah commands a remembrance of the Clouds of Glory and not of the mann, because bread and water are necessities, while the clouds were a gift of comfort that shows Hashem wants His people to be at ease.

The halachic requirement that rain can enter concerns the building of the sukkah; when rain did not enter the Ba'al Shem Tov's sukkah, the sechach still let it in and the Ba'al Shem Tov kept it out, so the two do not conflict.

The word simcha is bound up with leaning on Hashem: the one who relies on Him is calm and lacks nothing, while the passuk's 'ne'ezav', forsaken, is read as sad, since being alone with no one to lean on is the opposite of simcha.

The Ba'al Shem Tov did not intend a miracle when rain stayed out of his sukkah; he sat with the feeling of truly being under the wings of the Shechinah, as the Jews were in the desert, and that is the true mitzvah of sukkah.
Rabbi Zeira's derivation from a passuk about the days of Moshiach still stands, because a glimmer of that future shelter exists today in the sukkah of individual tzaddikim.

There is no contradiction between the Zohar, which reads 'betzilo chimadti' on the sukkah, and the Midrash, which reads it on the Beis HaMikdash, because the sukkah itself carries the holiness of the Beis HaMikdash.
Yaakov's kfitzas haderech meant that the Beis HaMikdash came to him in chutz la'aretz; in the same way the sukkah, which Yaakov founded, brings the Mikdash to every Jew wherever he is.

Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Eliezer agree that the miracle was the clouds of glory; Rabbi Akiva's 'actual sukkos' add that their protection left the camp with the soldiers, which is why they sat in flimsy huts at war instead of digging trenches.

The Rambam limits the bad sign of rain to the first night because the first meal is what establishes the sukkah as one's dwelling; once established, later rain is like a leak that does not change one's address.

Measurement belongs to the lowest level, malchus; the Torah measures the teivah, the Mishkan and the sukkah precisely because a light far above this world can only be drawn into it through a cheshbon.
Simcha is related to 'somech', having something firm to lean on, while atzvus comes from 'azuv', being forsaken; so joy grows from bitachon.

Since entering the sukkah is entering Eretz Yisrael and the Mikdash, the Gemara's rule that one who flees to Eretz Yisrael has his judgment reopened explains why the sealing of judgment extends beyond Yom Kippur.
The Mashgiach portrays the arba minim as weapons and ammunition in the heavenly war of Gog uMagog, with which Jews try to break through to Moshiach on Hoshana Rabbah.
Since the aravah resembles lips, the war of the day is fought not only with the species but with the heart and the mouth.
The diminishing bulls of Sukkos, ending today with the last of the seventy, are themselves part of the war of Gog uMagog: the nullification of the seventy nations that oppress the Shechinah.
The Mashgiach applies the passuk of the oppressed and the debtors who gathered around Dovid when he fled from Shaul to Hoshana Rabbah, the day of Dovid, when every Jew must gather around him.
The prosecutors in the war against Moshiach are armed with the sins of Jews, so even small matters such as talking during chazaras hashatz decide whether Moshiach comes closer.
The Chachamim who fixed the calendar so that Hoshana Rabbah never falls on Shabbos had in mind the low generations before Moshiach, whose souls are repaired by the mitzvah of aravah.
The generations follow the order of the four kinds: earlier generations were esrogim, then lulavim, then hadassim, and ours is the aravah.
The aravah is specifically a weekday mitzvah: on Shabbos the forces of impurity hide, but on a weekday they come out in strength and the aravah's power is needed to strike them.
On Hoshana Rabbah, when the last of the seventy bulls has been offered, the nations are at the height of their strength and wage the war of Gog uMagog in heaven to hold back Moshiach.
The people who gathered to Dovid, in distress, in debt and bitter of soul, are the souls of the last generation: those in debt from this and earlier lives, who feel they have done nothing for Hashem.
